01_Elements_compounds_and_mixtures.json.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
01_Elements_compounds_and_mixtures.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Classify a substance shown in a particle diagram, or described by its formula, as an element, a compound or a mixture.

Justify a classification by referring to whether the composition is fixed or variable and whether different particles are chemically bonded, and explain why physically separating a mixture does not break the chemical bonds inside its component substances.

prerequisites.statement: The particle model: a sample of matter is made of very many tiny particles, which can be single atoms or groups of atoms joined together (molecules).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Classifying a substance means classifying the particles inside it, not the visible lump of material.

prerequisites.statement: In a particle diagram, different coloured or shaped circles represent atoms of different elements.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading off whether a diagram shows one or several elements depends on noticing that convention.

diagnostic_items.question: A diagram shows six identical circles, none of them touching or joined to another. Is this an element, a compound or a mixture?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: An element, because every particle is the same type of atom and none are chemically joined to a different type.

common_wrong_answers.answer: A mixture, because the particles are separate and not joined.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats 'not joined' as the defining feature of a mixture, without first checking whether more than one type of particle is present.

common_wrong_answers.answer: A compound, because there is more than one particle.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner equates 'several particles' with 'several elements', ignoring that all six circles are identical.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner classifies by counting types of particle rather than counting particles or looking at bonding alone.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Cover the diagram and ask only 'how many different types of circle are there?' before asking about bonding; repeat with a diagram containing two identical pairs.

theory_blocks.title: Three samples, one question
theory_blocks.body:
Imagine three samples on a bench: a coil of pure copper wire, a lump of black copper oxide powder, and a jar of copper filings stirred together with sulfur powder. All three contain copper, yet chemists put them in three different categories, and the category depends on two questions asked about the particles inside each sample, not on how the sample looks.

First: how many different types of atom are present? Second, if there is more than one type: are they chemically joined (bonded) to each other, or just sitting together unjoined? The copper wire has one type of atom, so it is an **element**. The copper oxide has copper and oxygen atoms joined together in a fixed ratio, so it is a [[orange:**compound**]]. The copper-and-sulfur jar has two types of particle that are not joined to each other and could be mixed in any proportion, so it is a **mixture**.

theory_blocks.title: Defining element, compound and mixture
theory_blocks.body:
- An **element** contains only one type of atom. It may exist as separate single atoms (most metals) or as molecules made of that one type of atom joined together, such as $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, $\mathrm{N_{2}}$, $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$.
- A **compound** contains two or more different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Its formula states that ratio exactly: water, $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, is always two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom, never any other ratio.
- A **mixture** contains two or more substances (elements, compounds, or both) together without new chemical bonds forming between them. The proportions can vary, and each substance keeps its own individual properties.

The diagram below shows four particle arrangements built from the same two colours of atom, so that only composition and bonding — never colour — decide the category.

assets.caption: Four particle diagrams built from the same two atom colours: an element as single atoms, an element as paired atoms, a compound, and a mixture.
assets.purpose: Shows that classification depends on composition and bonding, not on colour or on how many atoms are in one particle.

theory_blocks.title: A molecule of one element is still an element
theory_blocks.body: Panel two of the figure above is easy to mis-read as a compound, because it shows two atoms joined together. Look again: both atoms in each pair are the same colour, so only one element is present. Oxygen gas, $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, chlorine gas, $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$, and nitrogen gas, $\mathrm{N_{2}}$, are all elements for exactly this reason — their particles are molecules, but every atom inside each molecule is identical.

theory_blocks.title: Separating a mixture breaks no bond
theory_blocks.body:
Filtering muddy water, evaporating salt water, or using a magnet to pull iron filings out of a sand-and-iron mixture are all **physical** processes. Each one relies on a physical difference — particle size, solubility, or magnetism — to pull substances apart; [[red:none of them forms or breaks a chemical bond]].

You can test this directly: evaporate salt water and the white solid left behind looks the same as the salt you started with and has the same melting point as the salt you started with. No new substance has appeared, so nothing was chemically changed; the water and the salt had simply been sitting together unbonded all along.

keywords.definition: A substance made of only one type of atom.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio.
Two or more substances together, not chemically bonded, in proportions that can vary.
Two or more atoms joined together by chemical bonds; the atoms may be the same element or different elements.
A method such as filtration, evaporation or distillation that separates substances using a physical property, without breaking chemical bonds.

worked_examples.statement: **Three samples of copper.** Sample A is pure copper wire. Sample B is black copper oxide powder, made of copper and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Sample C is copper filings stirred together with sulfur powder, in no particular ratio. Classify each sample.
solution: Sample A: only copper atoms are present, so it is an **element**.
Sample B: two different elements (copper and oxygen) are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, so it is a **compound**.
Sample C: two substances are present together with no fixed ratio and no new bond between them, so it is a **mixture**.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same element, copper, appears in all three samples; the category depends entirely on what else is present and whether it is bonded, not on the copper itself.

worked_examples.statement: **Is oxygen gas a compound?** A particle diagram shows pairs of identical circles, none touching any other pair. A student says this must be a compound because each particle contains two atoms. Decide whether the student is correct.
solution: Count the number of different atom types shown: every circle in the diagram is the same colour, so only one element is present.
A compound requires at least two different elements chemically bonded together; having two atoms is not enough on its own.
The diagram represents a molecular element, such as $\mathrm{O_{2}}$: the student is incorrect.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Counting atoms in a particle before checking whether they are all the same element.

worked_examples.statement: **Salt water under the microscope.** A student argues that salt water must be a compound, 'because once you mix them the salt and the water seem stuck together and you can't easily tell them apart.' Evaluate this claim, and describe a method that would settle the argument.
solution: A compound is defined by a fixed ratio of chemically bonded elements; salt water can be made weaker or stronger by adding more or less salt, so there is no fixed ratio.
'Hard to tell apart by eye' is not evidence of bonding: particles can be too small to see individually while still remaining physically, not chemically, combined.

Evaporate a sample of the salt water. If the water boils away and leaves behind dry salt with the same appearance and melting point as the salt that was added, no new substance has been formed and no chemical bond has been broken, so salt water is a mixture, not a compound.
worked_examples.interpretation: Recovering the unchanged salt by evaporation is the practical test that distinguishes a mixture (components recoverable unchanged) from a compound (would require a chemical reaction to recover the elements).

guided_exercises.statement: A particle diagram shows four green circles, each joined to a blue circle next to it, forming four identical green-blue pairs; no other particles are present. Classify this substance and justify your answer.
hints: First decide how many different atom colours are shown.
Then decide whether those different atoms are joined (bonded) to each other.
Finally check whether the ratio of the two colours is the same in every pair.
guided_exercises.answer: This is a **compound**: two different elements (green and blue) are chemically bonded together, and every particle has exactly the same 1:1 ratio of green to blue.
common_errors: Calling this a mixture because there are two colours, without first checking that the two colours are actually joined together in every particle.

guided_exercises.statement: A sample of sand and salt is mixed together and then stirred into water. Describe a method to recover dry, unchanged salt from this mixture, and explain why this method does not change the chemical identity of either the sand or the salt.
hints: Sand does not dissolve in water, but salt does: use that physical difference first.
Once the sand is removed, the remaining salt solution needs a method that removes the water without removing the salt.
At every stage, ask whether you are using a physical property (particle size, solubility, boiling point) or forming a new bond.
guided_exercises.answer: Filter the mixture: the insoluble sand is trapped on the filter paper while the salt solution passes through. Then evaporate the filtered solution to boil off the water, leaving dry salt crystals behind. These are physical separation methods: no new substances form, so the sand and salt retain their chemical identities.
common_errors: Describing evaporation as 'breaking down' the salt, rather than only removing the water that was mixed with it.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Filter the mixture: the insoluble sand is trapped on the filter paper while the salt solution passes through. Then evaporate the filtered solution to boil off the water, leaving dry salt crystals behind. These are physical separation methods: no new substances form, so the sand and salt retain their chemical identities.

exercises.statement: Classify each of the following as an element, a compound or a mixture, giving one reason for each: (a) $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ gas, (b) $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ gas, (c) air (mostly $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, in proportions that vary slightly with location), (d) solid sodium chloride, $\mathrm{NaCl}$.
exercises.answer: (a) Element: only nitrogen atoms are present, as $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ molecules. (b) Compound: carbon and oxygen are chemically bonded in the fixed ratio 1:2. (c) Mixture: several substances (mainly nitrogen and oxygen) together in a proportion that is not fixed by a chemical rule. (d) Compound: sodium and chlorine are chemically bonded in a fixed 1:1 ratio.

exercises.statement: Ozone, $\mathrm{O_{3}}$, is a gas found high in the atmosphere, with three oxygen atoms joined in one molecule. Explain why ozone is classified as an element and not a compound.
exercises.answer: Ozone is an element because every atom in the $\mathrm{O_{3}}$ molecule is the same element, oxygen. A compound requires at least two different elements to be chemically bonded together; having three atoms in one particle does not by itself make a substance a compound.

exercises.statement: Bronze is made by melting copper and tin together; a maker can use anywhere from about 5% to 20% tin depending on the properties wanted, and the copper and tin atoms do not combine in a fixed ratio to form a new compound. Classify bronze and justify your answer using the idea of fixed versus variable composition.
exercises.answer: Bronze is a mixture (specifically an alloy): the ratio of copper to tin is not fixed by any chemical rule and can be deliberately varied, and copper and tin are not chemically bonded together into a new compound.
common_errors: Assuming that because bronze looks and behaves differently from pure copper, it must be a compound; a mixture's properties can still differ from those of its separate components.

exercises.statement: A can of fizzy drink contains water, dissolved sugar ($\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}$), and dissolved carbon dioxide gas ($\mathrm{CO_{2}}$). Classify the drink as a whole, then classify each of the three substances named inside it, explaining your reasoning for one of them in detail.
exercises.answer: The drink as a whole is a mixture: three substances are present together, none chemically bonded to each other, in proportions that could be varied (more or less sugar, more or less fizz). Water ($\mathrm{H_{2}O}$) and sugar ($\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}$) are both compounds, since each is made of different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_{2}}$) is also a compound, for the same reason: one carbon atom is bonded to two oxygen atoms in every molecule, a ratio that never changes, which is exactly what marks it out as a compound rather than a mixture of carbon and oxygen.

exam_questions.statement: Three unlabelled gas jars contain: (i) pure nitrogen gas, (ii) ammonia gas, $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$, (iii) a mixture of nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas. Describe, in terms of the particles present, how sample (ii) differs from samples (i) and (iii), and explain how (i) and (iii) could be told apart without doing a chemical test.
exam_questions.answer: Sample (ii), ammonia, is a compound: it contains two different elements, nitrogen and hydrogen, chemically bonded together in the fixed ratio of one nitrogen atom to three hydrogen atoms. Samples (i) and (iii) both contain only nitrogen and/or hydrogen atoms, not bonded into a new compound, so they are not compounds. Sample (i), pure nitrogen, contains only one type of particle ($\mathrm{N_{2}}$ molecules); sample (iii) contains two types of particle ($\mathrm{N_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ molecules) mixed in a proportion that is not fixed. Without a chemical test, (i) and (iii) could be distinguished by measuring the density of each gas sample: a pure gas has one fixed density, while the mixture's density would depend on exactly how much hydrogen (a much less dense gas) had been added.
mark_scheme: Identifies ammonia as a compound because it contains two different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
States that samples (i) and (iii) do not contain a new compound.
Identifies that (i) has one type of particle and (iii) has two types of particle present together.
Gives a valid physical (non-chemical) method to distinguish (i) from (iii), such as comparing density, with a reason.

exam_questions.statement: A sample of muddy water (sand suspended in water that also contains a dissolved solid) is filtered, and the clear water that passes through is then evaporated to leave a white solid behind. Explain, with reference to chemical bonds, why neither the filtering step nor the evaporation step chemically changes the sand or the dissolved solid.
exam_questions.answer: Filtering separates the mud (an insoluble solid, made of particles too large to pass through the filter paper) from the water and dissolved solid using only particle size; this is a physical process and forms or breaks no chemical bonds within the mud itself. Evaporation removes the water by giving its particles enough energy to escape as vapour, leaving the dissolved solid behind; the bonds inside the water molecules and inside the dissolved solid's own particles are unaffected, because evaporation only overcomes the weaker physical attractions holding the mixture's components together, not the chemical bonds inside each substance. Since no new substance appears at either stage, both the sand and the white solid keep their original chemical identity throughout.
mark_scheme: States that filtering separates by particle size (a physical property).
States that this does not break the chemical bonds inside the sand's particles.
States that evaporation removes water by energy input, not by a chemical change.
States that the bonds inside the dissolved solid are unaffected by evaporation.
Concludes that no new substance is formed at either step, so both processes are physical.

mcq.stem: Which of the following is a compound?

options.text: $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$
$\mathrm{O_{2}}$
options.why_wrong: this contains only one element, oxygen, so it is a molecular element, not a compound.

options.text: A mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder
options.why_wrong: the two substances are not chemically bonded and can be mixed in any proportion.

options.text: Air
options.why_wrong: air is several gases together in proportions that are not fixed by a chemical formula.

mcq.explanation: $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ contains two different elements, carbon and oxygen, chemically bonded in the fixed ratio 1:2.

mcq.stem: A particle diagram shows separate pairs of joined, identical purple circles. What does this diagram represent?

options.text: A compound
options.why_wrong: a compound needs at least two different elements; every atom shown here is identical.

options.text: An element made of molecules
A mixture of two elements
options.why_wrong: only one colour of circle is present, so only one element is shown.

options.text: It cannot be classified without knowing the element's name
options.why_wrong: classification only needs the number of different particle types and whether they are bonded, both of which are already shown.

mcq.explanation: All the atoms are identical, so only one element is present; it simply happens to exist as two-atom molecules, like $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ or $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$.

mcq.stem: Which statement about mixtures is correct?

options.text: A mixture always contains its components in a fixed ratio.
options.why_wrong: a fixed ratio is the defining feature of a compound, not a mixture.

options.text: A mixture must contain at least one element and at least one compound.
options.why_wrong: a mixture can be formed from two elements, two compounds, or a mix of both.

options.text: A mixture can contain its components in any proportion.
A mixture always forms a new chemical bond between its components.
options.why_wrong: forming a new chemical bond would make the result a compound, not a mixture.

mcq.explanation: Mixtures have no fixed composition; the proportion of each substance present can vary, unlike in a compound.

mcq.stem: Salt is dissolved in water and the water is then evaporated, leaving dry salt behind. What does this show about the salt and water in the original mixture?

options.text: A chemical bond between the salt and water was broken by heating.
options.why_wrong: if a bond had been broken, a new substance would have been produced; instead the original salt reappears unchanged.

options.text: The salt was chemically changed into a new substance by the water.
options.why_wrong: the recovered solid still behaves exactly like the original salt, so no new substance has been made.

options.text: The experiment proves that salt water is a compound.
options.why_wrong: recovering the unchanged salt is evidence against this; a compound could not be separated back into its original form just by evaporation.

options.text: No chemical bond had formed between the salt and the water.

mcq.explanation: Because the same salt is recovered unchanged, no chemical bond between the salt and the water can have existed or been broken; they were only ever physically mixed.

flashcards.front: What is an element?
flashcards.back: A substance containing only one type of atom.

flashcards.front: What is a compound?
flashcards.back: Two or more different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio.

flashcards.front: How does the composition of a mixture differ from the composition of a compound?
flashcards.back: A compound has a fixed ratio of elements fixed by its formula; a mixture's components can be present in any proportion.

flashcards.front: Is a molecule of nitrogen gas, $\mathrm{N_{2}}$, a compound?
flashcards.back: No. Both atoms are nitrogen, so only one element is present; it is a molecular element, not a compound.

flashcards.front: You evaporate salt water and recover unchanged dry salt. What does this tell you about salt water?
flashcards.back: No chemical bond existed between the salt and the water, because no bond was broken to recover the original salt; salt water is a mixture.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A mixture always has a fixed, definite composition, in the same way as a compound.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday mixtures that learners meet first, such as a particular brand of fizzy drink, do taste the same every time, which hides the fact that the proportions were not fixed by any chemical rule.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a mixture using a single fixed ratio or refuses to accept that the same two substances could be mixed in different proportions.
misconceptions.correct_model: A mixture can contain its component substances in any proportion: salt water can be weak or strong, and air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen but the exact percentages are not fixed by a chemical law.
misconceptions.remediation: Make two cups of salt water with visibly different amounts of salt and ask whether both are still 'salt water'; contrast with water, H2O, which is always two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A molecule must always contain atoms of at least two different elements.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The first molecules many learners meet, such as water or carbon dioxide, do contain more than one element, so 'molecule' and 'compound' become linked in memory.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner classifies oxygen gas, O2, or nitrogen gas, N2, as a compound because the particle has more than one atom.
misconceptions.correct_model: A molecule is simply two or more atoms joined together; if every atom in it is the same element, the substance is still an element, just one whose particles happen to be pairs (or larger groups) rather than single atoms.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw O2 beside CO2 side by side and ask, for each, how many different colours of circle are present before asking for a name.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Physically separating the parts of a mixture breaks the chemical bonds inside each substance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Separating feels like an active, almost violent process (filtering, boiling), so learners assume something is being broken apart at the same scale as a chemical bond.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says evaporating salt water 'breaks down' the salt, or that filtering sand from water changes the sand into something new.
misconceptions.correct_model: Filtration, evaporation and distillation separate different substances from each other using only differences in physical properties (particle size, boiling point); they do not break the bonds that hold the particles of any one substance together.
misconceptions.remediation: Evaporate salt water, recover dry salt, and ask whether the recovered solid still looks and behaves like salt; if no new substance has appeared, no chemical bond was broken.

common_mistakes.mistake: Classifying any particle with more than one atom as a compound.
common_mistakes.why: Learners link 'more than one atom' with 'more than one element' without checking.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always count the number of different colours/types of atom first; a molecule of one element, such as $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, is still an element.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a mixture as having a fixed composition.
common_mistakes.why: Familiar mixtures (a particular drink, a particular alloy) taste or behave consistently, which hides that the ratio was a choice, not a chemical rule.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether the two substances could, in principle, be combined in a different proportion and still be given the same general name.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming physical separation changes the chemical identity of a substance.
common_mistakes.why: Separation methods (filtering, evaporating) look dramatic and are confused with chemical change.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether a new substance with new properties has appeared; if not, no chemical bond has been broken or formed.

exam_notes: When classifying a substance, state explicitly how many different elements are present and whether they are chemically bonded, rather than just naming the category.
A formula with a subscript on a single element symbol, such as $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ or $\mathrm{P_{4}}$, always represents an element, however many atoms are in the molecule.
When asked to distinguish a mixture from a compound using an experiment, describe a physical method (density, boiling point, solubility) and explain what result would support each conclusion.

summary.big_idea: Whether a substance is an element, a compound or a mixture depends on how many different elements are present and whether they are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
key_points: An element has one type of atom, whether as single atoms or as molecules of that one element.
A compound has two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, shown by its formula.
A mixture has substances together in a proportion that is not fixed, with no new bond between them.
Physical separation methods never break the chemical bonds inside a substance's own particles.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Count the types of atom, then check whether different types are bonded in a fixed ratio: that single check sorts element, compound and mixture.

exit_check.question: A gas jar contains only $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$ molecules. A student says this must be a compound because each particle has two atoms. What is wrong with this reasoning, and what is the gas actually?
exit_check.answer: Having two atoms in a particle does not make a substance a compound; a compound needs two different elements. Both atoms in $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$ are chlorine, so the gas is an element, chlorine, existing as diatomic molecules.

02_Atomic_structure_electrons_and_isotop.title: Atomic structure, electrons and isotopes
02_Atomic_structure_electrons_and_isotop.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe the structure of an atom in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons, state their relative charges and masses, and calculate proton number and mass number for atoms with Z up to 20.

Work out the electron configuration of an atom with proton number 1-20 using the shell pattern 2,8,8, and relate the number of outer-shell electrons to group number and the number of occupied shells to period number.
Interpret isotope and ion notation, distinguish an isotope from an ion, and explain why isotopes of the same element react in chemically similar ways.
Interpret and use nuclide symbols for atoms and for ions, deducing the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from a symbol, and writing the symbol for a given set of counts.

prerequisites.statement: An element is identified by the type of atom it contains.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Proton number is what makes that identification precise and numerical.

prerequisites.statement: Subtract one whole number from another, including when the answer could be mistaken for the wrong one of the two starting numbers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the number of neutrons, or the number of outer electrons remaining in a shell, is a subtraction every time.

prerequisites.statement: Read the group and period position of an element directly from a periodic table.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Group and period numbers are compared against the electron configuration calculated in this lesson.

diagnostic_items.question: One sealed jar holds particles that are all the same type of atom. A second jar holds particles made of two different types of atom chemically joined together. Which jar holds an element, and what feature of the contents decides it?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The first jar holds an element, because it contains only one type of atom. What decides it is the number of different types of atom present, not how many particles there are or whether the atoms are joined to each other.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The second jar, because it contains more particles.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner classifies by counting particles rather than counting types of atom, so will later also struggle to see why proton number alone fixes the element.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Neither, because in an element the atoms must be separate and unjoined.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats being joined as disqualifying, and will reject the idea that a sample of joined atoms of one kind is still a single element.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner identifies an element by the single type of atom present, which this lesson makes numerical by replacing "type of atom" with "proton number".
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Re-sort three particle diagrams from an earlier lesson into element, compound and mixture, saying aloud how many different types of atom each one contains, before starting this lesson.

diagnostic_items.question: Work out $23-11$ and $40-20$ without a calculator, then say which of your two answers is equal to one of the numbers it was calculated from.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $23-11=12$ and $40-20=20$. The second answer, 20, is equal to one of the numbers it was calculated from, and that is perfectly normal.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner copies the number being subtracted instead of carrying out the subtraction, which in this lesson turns into "neutrons = proton number" for every atom.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $40-20$ cannot be 20, because an answer may not repeat a number from the question.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner expects a subtraction to produce a new number and so distrusts a correct result, which leads to inventing a different neutron count for calcium-40.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner subtracts confidently even when the answer coincides with one of the starting numbers, which is exactly the case for calcium-40 and every other atom with equal numbers of protons and neutrons.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise five subtractions of the form $A-Z$ with mixed answers, including two where the answer equals $Z$, checking each one by adding the answer back to $Z$.

theory_blocks.title: What is actually inside an atom
theory_blocks.body:
An atom has a tiny, dense **nucleus** at its centre, containing **protons** (charge +1) and **neutrons** (no charge), surrounded by **electrons** (charge -1) occupying the much larger space around the nucleus. A proton and a neutron have almost the same mass; an electron's mass is so small (about 1/2000 of a proton's) that it is normally ignored when adding up an atom's mass.

Two counting rules follow directly from this picture. The [[blue:**proton number**]] (or atomic number), $Z$, counts the protons, and it is what makes one element different from every other element: change $Z$ and you have changed the element. The **mass number**, $A$, counts protons plus neutrons together. For a neutral atom (no overall charge), the number of electrons always equals the number of protons, because the atom's negative and positive charges must balance.

theory_blocks.title: Finding protons, neutrons and electrons from Z and A
theory_blocks.body:
Given proton number $Z$ and mass number $A$ for a neutral atom:

$$\text{protons} = Z, \qquad \text{electrons} = Z, \qquad \text{neutrons} = A - Z.$$

For sodium, $Z=11$ and $A=23$: protons $=11$, electrons $=11$, and neutrons $=23-11=12$. Checking by addition, $11+12=23$, which returns the mass number, confirming the subtraction. This rearrangement only ever subtracts the smaller number ($Z$) from the larger ($A$); mass number can never be smaller than proton number, because neutron number cannot be negative.

assets.caption: Nuclide notation for sodium-23: mass number and atomic number read off, with the neutron and electron counts calculated from them.
assets.purpose: Shows exactly where each of the four counted quantities (protons, neutrons, mass number, electrons) comes from in the symbol.

theory_blocks.title: Filling electron shells, Z = 1 to 20
theory_blocks.body:
Electrons occupy **shells** around the nucleus, filling them from the innermost shell outward. For proton numbers 1 to 20, the shells fill in a simple pattern: the first shell holds up to 2 electrons, the second up to 8, and the third up to 8 (after which the fourth shell starts, holding 2 for potassium and calcium). Configurations are written as the electrons in each shell separated by commas, innermost first: sodium ($Z=11$) is $2,8,1$; chlorine ($Z=17$) is $2,8,7$; calcium ($Z=20$) is $2,8,8,2$.

Two patterns fall straight out of this filling rule. The number of electrons in the **outer** (last-written) shell equals the **group number** for groups I-VII, and a full outer shell of 8 (or 2, for helium) is group VIII/0. The number of shells written down (however many numbers appear) equals the **period number**. Sodium, $2,8,1$, is group I (one outer electron) and period 3 (three shells); chlorine, $2,8,7$, is group VII and period 3.

assets.caption: Shell diagrams for sodium (2,8,1) and chlorine (2,8,7), drawn with the same shell-ring convention used throughout this unit.
assets.purpose: Gives a visual anchor for shell filling that is reused unchanged when sodium and chlorine form ions in the next lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Isotope or ion: which number changed?
theory_blocks.body:
Two particles of the same element can differ from the 'standard' atom in two completely different ways, and keeping them apart matters.

**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element (same $Z$, so the same number of protons and electrons) with a **different number of neutrons**, so a different mass number. Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are both chlorine ($Z=17$ in both), but chlorine-35 has $35-17=18$ neutrons while chlorine-37 has $37-17=20$ neutrons. Because chemical reactions are governed almost entirely by the outer-shell electrons, and isotopes of the same element have identical electron configurations, isotopes react in essentially the same chemical way; only their mass, and properties that depend on mass, differ measurably.

An **ion**, by contrast, has a different number of **electrons** from protons, giving it an overall charge, while its proton number (and therefore which element it is) and its neutron number stay exactly as they were. A sodium ion, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, still has 11 protons; it simply has 10 electrons instead of 11, one fewer than a neutral sodium atom.

theory_blocks.title: Going further: nuclide symbols for atoms and ions
theory_blocks.body:
A nuclide symbol packs these counts into one piece of notation. The element symbol carries the mass number $A$ as a superscript on its left, the proton number $Z$ as a subscript below that, and any charge as a superscript on its right:

$$^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}^{n\pm}$$

Read it in three steps: $Z$ gives the protons; $A-Z$ gives the neutrons; the electron count starts from $Z$ and is then adjusted for the charge, because a charge of $n+$ means $n$ electrons fewer than protons and a charge of $n-$ means $n$ electrons more.

So $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl^-}$ has 17 protons, $35-17=18$ neutrons and $17+1=18$ electrons, while $^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ has 12 protons, $24-12=12$ neutrons and $12-2=10$ electrons. Writing a symbol is the same steps in reverse: an atom with 8 protons and 10 neutrons has $Z=8$, so it is oxygen, and $A=8+10=18$, giving $^{18}_{8}\mathrm{O}$.

keywords.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus; it identifies the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
A region around the nucleus where electrons are arranged, filled in a fixed order.
An atom of an element with the same proton number but a different neutron number from another atom of that element.
A charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons, so that electron number no longer equals proton number.

worked_examples.statement: **Counting sodium's particles.** An atom of sodium has proton number 11 and mass number 23. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
solution: Protons $=Z=11$.
Electrons $=$ protons (neutral atom) $=11$.
Neutrons $=A-Z=23-11=12$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $11+12=23$, the given mass number.

worked_examples.statement: **Electron configuration and periodic position of aluminium.** Aluminium has proton number 13. Work out its electron configuration, and state its group and period.
reasoning: Fill the first shell: 2 electrons placed, 11 remaining.
Fill the second shell: 8 electrons placed, 3 remaining.
Place the remaining 3 electrons in the third shell: configuration $2,8,3$.
The outer shell has 3 electrons, so aluminium is in group III; three shells are occupied, so it is in period 3.
solution: Configuration: $2,8,3$.
Group III, period 3.
worked_examples.interpretation: $2+8+3=13$, matching the proton number, so every electron has been placed exactly once.

worked_examples.statement: **Same element, different mass.** Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are both found in nature. Determine the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in each, and explain why both react with sodium to form the same compound, sodium chloride.
solution: Both are chlorine, so both have $Z=17$: 17 protons and (neutral atoms) 17 electrons in each.
Chlorine-35: neutrons $=35-17=18$.
Chlorine-37: neutrons $=37-17=20$.
Both isotopes have the identical electron configuration, $2,8,7$, because electron number depends only on proton number, not on neutron number.

Chemical bonding depends on the outer-shell electrons, which are identical for both isotopes, so both react with sodium in the same way to form sodium chloride; the extra two neutrons in chlorine-37 change its mass but not its chemistry.
worked_examples.interpretation: $17+18=35$ and $17+20=37$: both mass numbers check out against the given isotope names.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading two nuclide symbols.** State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl^-}$ and in $^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$.
solution: $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl^-}$: protons $=Z=17$; neutrons $=A-Z=35-17=18$.
The charge is $1-$, so there is one electron more than there are protons: electrons $=17+1=18$.
The charge is $2+$, so there are two electrons fewer than protons: electrons $=12-2=10$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both ions end up with 18 and 10 electrons respectively, the electron counts of argon and neon; the charge, not the mass number, is what changes the electron count.

worked_examples.statement: **Distinguishing an isotope from an ion.** A potassium atom has 19 protons, 19 electrons and 20 neutrons. Particle X has 19 protons, 18 electrons and 20 neutrons. Particle Y has 19 protons, 19 electrons and 22 neutrons. Identify X and Y, giving a reason for each.
solution: Particle X: proton number (19) and neutron number (20) match the original potassium atom, but electron number (18) does not match proton number, so X carries a charge of $+1$. X is a potassium ion, $\mathrm{K^+}$.

Particle Y: proton number (19) matches, electron number (19) equals proton number so Y is neutral, but neutron number (22) differs from the original atom's 20. Y is an isotope of potassium, with mass number $19+22=41$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same proton number (19) is shared by the atom, X and Y throughout, confirming all three are potassium in some form; only the electron count (for X) or the neutron count (for Y) has changed.

guided_exercises.statement: Magnesium has proton number 12 and mass number 24. Work out its electron configuration and state its group and period.
hints: Fill the first shell with up to 2 electrons, then move to the next shell.
Keep a running total of electrons placed so far and electrons remaining.
Group comes from the last number written; period comes from how many numbers you wrote.
guided_exercises.answer: Configuration $2,8,2$; group II, period 3 (because $2+8+2=12$ matches the proton number, with 2 electrons in the outer shell and 3 shells occupied).
common_errors: Writing $2,8,2$ but then reading the group from the total number of shells (3) instead of from the outer-shell electron count (2).

guided_exercises.statement: An atom has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. A second particle of the same element has 20 protons, 18 electrons and 22 neutrons. Identify what kind of particle the second one is relative to the first, and find its mass number.
hints: Compare proton numbers first: if they match, it is still the same element.
Then compare electron number to proton number to check for a charge.
Finally compare neutron number to the original, to check for an isotope difference.
guided_exercises.answer: The second particle is both an isotope (different neutron number: 22 instead of 20) and an ion (18 electrons instead of 20 protons, giving a $2+$ charge). Its mass number is $20+22=42$.
common_errors: Stopping after spotting only the charge difference, and missing that the neutron number has also changed.

exercises.statement: Silicon has proton number 14 and mass number 28. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons, and write its electron configuration.
exercises.answer: Protons $=14$, electrons $=14$, neutrons $=28-14=14$. Configuration: $2,8,4$.

exercises.statement: Argon has electron configuration $2,8,8$. State its group and period, and explain in terms of its outer shell why argon is chemically unreactive.
exercises.answer: Argon is in group VIII/0 and period 3. Its outer shell already holds a full 8 electrons, so it has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, which is why it is chemically unreactive (a noble gas).

exercises.statement: Potassium-39 and potassium-40 are both isotopes of potassium ($Z=19$). Calculate the number of neutrons in each, and state one property that would be identical in both and one that would differ.
exercises.answer: Potassium-39: neutrons $=39-19=20$. Potassium-40: neutrons $=40-19=21$. Both have the identical electron configuration ($2,8,8,1$) and so react chemically in the same way; their mass (and mass-dependent properties, such as the precise mass of a fixed number of atoms) differs.

exercises.statement: (a) Write the nuclide symbol for an atom with 8 protons and 10 neutrons. (b) State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in $^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$.
exercises.answer: (a) $Z=8$, so the element is oxygen, and $A=8+10=18$: the symbol is $^{18}_{8}\mathrm{O}$. (b) Protons $=20$; neutrons $=40-20=20$; the $2+$ charge means two electrons fewer than protons, so electrons $=20-2=18$.

exercises.statement: A newly-discovered particle has 15 protons, 15 electrons and 16 neutrons. Without being told the element's name, predict its group and period from its proton number alone, and state the mass number of this particle.
exercises.answer: Build the configuration from $Z=15$: $2,8,5$. Outer shell has 5 electrons, so group V; three shells occupied, so period 3 (this is phosphorus, though the name is not needed to answer). Mass number $=15+16=31$.

exam_questions.statement: An atom of calcium has proton number 20 and mass number 40. (a) State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom. (b) Work out its electron configuration. (c) A calcium ion, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, forms when this atom reacts. State the number of electrons in this ion and explain why its proton number is unchanged.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Protons $=20$, neutrons $=40-20=20$, electrons $=20$. (b) $2,8,8,2$. (c) The ion has $20-2=18$ electrons; its proton number stays at 20 because forming an ion only ever removes or adds electrons, never protons, so the element's identity cannot change.
mark_scheme: States protons = 20.
Correctly calculates neutrons = 20.
States electrons = 20 for the neutral atom.
Gives the correct configuration 2,8,8,2.
States 18 electrons for $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ with a correct reason that forming an ion does not change proton number.

exam_questions.statement: Boron has two naturally occurring isotopes, boron-10 and boron-11. Explain what the term isotope means, using boron as your example, and state one way in which the chemistry of the two isotopes is the same and one way their physical properties differ.
exam_questions.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (the same proton number, here $Z=5$ for both) with different numbers of neutrons: boron-10 has $10-5=5$ neutrons and boron-11 has $11-5=6$ neutrons. Because both isotopes have the identical electron configuration ($2,3$), they react chemically in the same way. Their physical properties differ in anything that depends on mass, such as the mass of a fixed number of atoms (each boron-11 atom is heavier than a boron-10 atom), so, for example, pure samples of the two isotopes would have different densities.
mark_scheme: Defines isotopes as same proton number, different neutron number.
Calculates 5 neutrons for boron-10 and 6 for boron-11.
States that chemistry is the same because electron configuration is identical.
Gives a valid physical property that differs, linked to mass.

challenge_questions.statement: A particle has a proton number of 16, carries a charge of $2-$, and has 18 neutrons. A second particle has the same element's proton number, is neutral, and has a mass number 2 greater than the first particle's. Find, for the second particle, its number of electrons and its number of neutrons, explaining each step.
hints: Work out the first particle's electron number and mass number before touching the second particle.
The second particle shares only the proton number with the first; nothing else can be assumed equal.
challenge_questions.answer: First particle: $Z=16$ (sulfur), neutrons $=18$, so mass number $=16+18=34$; charge $2-$ means 2 more electrons than protons, so electrons $=16+2=18$. Second particle: same element, so $Z=16$; it is neutral, so electrons $=16$; its mass number is $34+2=36$, so neutrons $=36-16=20$.
common_errors: Carrying over the first particle's electron count (18) into the second particle, forgetting that the second particle is stated to be neutral.

mcq.stem: An atom has proton number 9 and mass number 19. How many neutrons does it have?

options.why_wrong: this is the proton number, not the number of neutrons.
this is the mass number, which already includes the protons.
this adds proton number and mass number instead of subtracting.

mcq.explanation: Neutrons $=A-Z=19-9=10$.

mcq.stem: An atom has the electron configuration $2,8,6$. What is its group and period?

options.text: Group II, period 6
options.why_wrong: this reads the group from the first number written (2) and the period from the outer-shell number (6); the group is the outer-shell count and the period is the number of shells.

options.text: Group VI, period 3
Group III, period 6
options.why_wrong: this swaps which number gives the group and reads the period from the outer electron count.

options.text: Group VI, period 6
options.why_wrong: this correctly finds the group but takes the period from the outer-shell count (6) instead of from the number of occupied shells (3).

mcq.explanation: The outer shell has 6 electrons (group VI); three numbers are written, so three shells are occupied (period 3).

mcq.stem: Which statement about two isotopes of the same element is correct?

options.text: They have different numbers of protons.
options.why_wrong: isotopes of the same element always share the identical proton number; a different proton number means a different element entirely.

options.text: They have different numbers of electrons in a neutral atom.
options.why_wrong: for neutral atoms, electron number always equals proton number, which is identical for isotopes.

options.text: They have different numbers of neutrons.
They react with other substances in completely different ways.
options.why_wrong: because their electron configurations are identical, isotopes of the same element react chemically in the same way.

mcq.explanation: Isotopes share proton (and so electron) number but differ in neutron number, and therefore in mass number.

mcq.stem: A neutral atom of fluorine has 9 protons and 10 neutrons. What is the mass of this atom closest to, measured in the same relative units as a proton?

options.why_wrong: this counts only the neutrons and ignores the protons, which contribute equally to the mass.
this counts only the protons and ignores the neutrons, which contribute equally to mass.
this adds the 9 electrons as if each had the same mass as a proton ($9+10+9=28$); an electron's mass is only about 1/2000 of a proton's and is ignored.

mcq.explanation: Mass number $=$ protons $+$ neutrons $=9+10=19$; electron mass is negligible and is not included.

mcq.stem: How many electrons are there in the ion $^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$?

options.why_wrong: this is the proton number; the $3+$ charge means three electrons have been lost, so the electron count is no longer equal to it.
this adds the charge to the proton number instead of subtracting it; a positive charge means electrons are missing.
this is the number of neutrons, $27-13=14$, not the number of electrons.

mcq.explanation: The proton number is 13, and a charge of $3+$ means three electrons fewer than protons: $13-3=10$.

flashcards.front: How do you find the number of neutrons in an atom?
flashcards.back: Neutrons $=$ mass number $-$ proton number ($A-Z$).

flashcards.front: What is the shell-filling pattern used for proton numbers 1 to 20?
flashcards.back: $2$, then $8$, then $8$ (then a new shell begins, holding 2 for potassium and calcium).

flashcards.front: What does group number tell you, and what does period number tell you, about an electron configuration?
flashcards.back: Group number = number of outer-shell electrons; period number = number of occupied shells.

flashcards.front: Do two isotopes of the same element have different proton numbers?
flashcards.back: No. Isotopes share the same proton number; they differ only in neutron number (and therefore mass number).

flashcards.front: Why do isotopes of the same element react chemically in the same way?
flashcards.back: Chemical reactions depend on the outer-shell electrons, and isotopes of the same element have identical electron configurations; only neutron number (and mass) differs.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Isotopes of an element differ in the number of protons they contain.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes generalise 'isotopes are different versions of an atom' to mean that any particle in the atom could differ, rather than specifically the neutrons.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes carbon-12 and carbon-14 as having different proton numbers, or says changing proton number would still give 'an isotope of carbon'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Isotopes of the same element always have the identical proton number (that is what fixes the element); they differ only in neutron number, and therefore in mass number.
misconceptions.remediation: State explicitly that changing the proton number changes the element entirely, then show carbon-12 and carbon-14 side by side with protons highlighted as identical and only the neutron count different.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An electron has about the same mass as a proton.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners meet protons, neutrons and electrons together as 'the three particles in an atom' before being told how different their masses actually are, so all three can seem interchangeable in size.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner includes electron mass when calculating mass number, or says losing electrons would noticeably change an atom's mass.
misconceptions.correct_model: An electron has a mass about 1/2000 that of a proton or neutron, so mass number (protons + neutrons) ignores electrons entirely; forming an ion changes charge but not, to any measurable extent at this level, mass.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the relative mass table (proton 1, neutron 1, electron about 1/2000) and ask the learner to recalculate a mass number with and without the electrons to see that the answer does not change.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The group number tells you how many electron shells an atom has.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both group and period numbers are read from the same periodic table position, so the two separate meanings (outer electrons vs occupied shells) can be swapped by mistake.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says sodium (group I, period 3) has one shell, or that chlorine (group VII) has seven shells.
misconceptions.correct_model: Group number (for groups I-VII, and the full group VIII/0) tells you the number of electrons in the outer shell; period number tells you the number of occupied shells. Sodium, 2,8,1, is in group I because of its single outer electron, and in period 3 because it has three occupied shells.
misconceptions.remediation: Build the configuration first (shell by shell), then read off group from the last number and period from how many numbers were written down, always in that order.

common_mistakes.mistake: Subtracting proton number from mass number the wrong way round, or adding instead of subtracting.
common_mistakes.why: Mass number and proton number are easy to mix up when both are just written as plain numbers next to an element's symbol.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always write neutrons $=A-Z$ and check that mass number is the larger of the two before subtracting.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading group number from the number of shells and period number from the outer-shell electron count.
common_mistakes.why: Both numbers come from the same configuration, so which one means what is easy to swap.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the configuration first, then read group from the last number and period from the count of numbers written.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a different neutron number must also mean a different proton number.
common_mistakes.why: Isotope symbols change the mass number, which can look like 'a different element' at a glance.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the element's name or proton number explicitly before concluding anything has changed about the element itself.

exam_notes: Always show the subtraction $A-Z$ explicitly when finding neutrons; an unsupported final number earns no method mark if it is wrong.
When asked for 'electron configuration', write the full list of numbers (such as 2,8,1), not just the outer-shell number.
A question on isotopes nearly always wants both the shared quantity (proton number) stated and the differing quantity (neutron number) calculated.

summary.big_idea: Proton number fixes which element an atom is; electron configuration (built shell by shell) fixes its group and period; neutron number can vary between isotopes without changing the chemistry.
key_points: Protons = Z, electrons = Z (neutral atom), neutrons = A - Z.
Shells fill 2, then 8, then 8 for proton numbers 1 to 20.
Outer-shell electron count = group number; number of shells occupied = period number.
Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutron number; they react chemically the same way.
An ion has a different electron number from its proton number, but its proton number never changes.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Proton number never changes without changing the element; only neutron number (isotopes) or electron number (ions) can vary.

exit_check.question: An atom X has 17 protons, 17 electrons and 20 neutrons. A second particle Y has 17 protons, 18 electrons and 18 neutrons. Is Y an isotope of X, an ion of X, both, or neither?
exit_check.answer: Both. Y's electron number (18) differs from its proton number (17), giving it a $1-$ charge, so Y is an ion. Y's neutron number (18) also differs from X's (20), giving mass numbers of 35 and 37 respectively, so Y is also an isotope of the same element as X. The two differences are independent: one compares electrons to protons, the other compares neutron counts between particles.

03_Ionic_bonding_and_lattice_properties..title: Ionic bonding and lattice properties
03_Ionic_bonding_and_lattice_properties..subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe how electron transfer between a Group I metal atom and a Group VII non-metal atom forms oppositely charged ions (cations and anions), and draw a dot-and-cross diagram for these Group I/VII examples.
Describe the properties of ionic compounds: high melting and boiling points, good electrical conductivity when molten or aqueous but poor conductivity when solid, and general solubility in water.

Describe an ionic compound as a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction, and explain why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.
Explain why solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity but molten or dissolved ionic compounds do, in terms of the mobility of ions.
Extend ionic bonding to metal/non-metal ion pairs beyond Group I/VII (including 2+ and 3+ metal ions and 2- non-metal ions), and use charge balance to deduce a correct formula.

prerequisites.statement: Electron configuration and the idea of an outer (valence) shell, for proton numbers up to 20.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Ionic bonding is explained entirely in terms of what happens to the outer-shell electrons.

prerequisites.statement: The distinction between an atom and an ion: an ion's electron number differs from its proton number.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Forming an ionic bond is nothing more than two atoms both becoming ions at the same time.

theory_blocks.title: Giving away or taking an electron to reach a full shell
theory_blocks.body:
A Group I metal atom, such as sodium ($2,8,1$), is one electron away from a full outer shell if it loses its single outer electron, leaving a stable $2,8$ arrangement. A Group VII non-metal atom, such as chlorine ($2,8,7$), is one electron away from a full outer shell if it gains one electron, reaching $2,8,8$. When a sodium atom meets a chlorine atom, sodium transfers its outer electron directly to chlorine: both atoms end up with a full outer shell, but sodium is left with one fewer electron than protons (charge $1+$) and chlorine with one more electron than protons (charge $1-$).

The oppositely charged ions, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, then attract each other electrostatically: this electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is the [[blue:**ionic bond**]].

theory_blocks.title: Drawing the transfer with a dot-and-cross diagram
theory_blocks.body:
A dot-and-cross diagram for ionic bonding shows only the outer (valence) shell of each atom, using dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the other's, so that the origin of every electron in the final ions is traceable. Before transfer, sodium's single outer electron is shown as a dot on its own shell; chlorine's seven outer electrons are shown as crosses, with one gap. The transferred electron is drawn moving into that gap, and keeps its dot symbol even though it is now one of chlorine's electrons, which is exactly how the diagram proves where each electron in the finished ion came from.

After transfer, each ion is written inside square brackets with its charge shown outside: $\big[\mathrm{Na}\big]^{+}$ (empty outer shell, now $2,8$) and $\big[\mathrm{Cl}\big]^{-}$ (full outer shell of 8: seven crosses plus the one dot from sodium).

assets.caption: Electron transfer from sodium to chlorine: before transfer (separate atoms) and after transfer (the resulting ions, with the transferred electron still marked as a dot).
assets.purpose: Makes the origin of every electron in each finished ion traceable, which is the entire point of a dot-and-cross diagram.

theory_blocks.title: What ionic compounds are like
theory_blocks.body:
Whichever metal and non-metal are involved, ionic compounds share a short list of properties, and being able to state them is Core content.

- **High melting points and boiling points.** Sodium chloride, for example, has to be heated to about 800 °C before it melts.
- **Electrical conductivity that depends on the state.** They conduct electricity well when molten or dissolved in water, and poorly when solid.
- **Solubility.** They are generally soluble in water.

The two sections that follow explain *why* each of these follows from the structure of the solid, which is Supplement content; the list itself is worth learning on its own.

theory_blocks.title: A giant lattice, not a pair
theory_blocks.body:
The formula $\mathrm{NaCl}$ states the simplest whole-number ratio of ions, not the size of a 'molecule': there is no individual $\mathrm{NaCl}$ particle. In the solid, each $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ion is surrounded by several $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions, and each $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ion by several $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ions, in a repeating three-dimensional pattern called a **giant ionic lattice**.

Because every ion attracts several neighbours of opposite charge, and this pattern repeats enormously many times, melting or boiling an ionic lattice means overcoming a very large number of strong electrostatic attractions at once, not just one bond. That is why ionic compounds typically have high melting points and high boiling points, and why many are at least somewhat soluble in water, which has a strong enough attraction to individual ions to pull the lattice apart.

assets.caption: Part of a giant ionic lattice: positive and negative ions alternate in every direction, each surrounded by several ions of opposite charge.
assets.purpose: Directly contradicts the isolated-pair misconception by showing many neighbours per ion.

theory_blocks.title: Why conduction depends on state, not just on being ionic
theory_blocks.body:
Electrical conduction always needs charged particles that are free to move. In a **solid** ionic lattice, the ions are held tightly in fixed positions by the electrostatic attraction described above, so although charged ions are present, none of them can move: solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity.

When the same compound is **melted** or **dissolved** in water, the rigid lattice breaks apart and the ions themselves become free to move. It is the ions, not electrons, that then carry the current: positive ions drift towards the negative electrode and negative ions towards the positive electrode. This is the key contrast with metals (covered in an earlier lesson), where it is mobile electrons, not mobile ions, that carry the current.

theory_blocks.title: Going further: ions beyond Group I and VII
theory_blocks.body:
The same transfer idea extends to metals that lose two or three electrons, and non-metals that gain two electrons. Magnesium ($2,8,2$) loses both outer electrons to form $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ($2,8$); oxygen ($2,6$) gains two electrons to form $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ($2,8$). Aluminium ($2,8,3$) loses three electrons to form $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ ($2,8$).

Because compounds are electrically neutral overall, the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge, and this charge balance fixes the formula. Magnesium oxide needs one $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ for every one $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ($+2-2=0$): $\mathrm{MgO}$. Magnesium chloride needs one $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ for every two $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ($+2+(-1)+(-1)=0$): $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$. Aluminium oxide needs two $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ for every three $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ($2(+3)+3(-2)=6-6=0$): $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$.

assets.caption: Dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium oxide: both of magnesium’s outer electrons transfer to one oxygen atom, giving a 2+ ion with an empty outer shell and a 2- ion with a full one.
assets.purpose: Gives the Supplement dot-and-cross example beyond Group I/VII (C2.4.5), where two electrons transfer at once rather than one.

keywords.definition: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains one or more electrons.
A repeating three-dimensional structure of alternating positive and negative ions.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles.

worked_examples.statement: **Forming sodium and chloride ions.** Sodium ($2,8,1$) reacts with chlorine ($2,8,7$). State what happens to the outer electron of sodium, and give the resulting electron configuration and charge of each ion formed.
solution: Sodium's single outer electron transfers to chlorine.
Sodium ion: configuration $2,8$, charge $+1$ (one fewer electron than protons).
Chloride ion: configuration $2,8,8$, charge $-1$ (one more electron than protons).
worked_examples.interpretation: Charge check: $(+1)+(-1)=0$, so sodium chloride is electrically neutral overall, as any ionic compound must be.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining a high melting point.** Sodium chloride melts at a much higher temperature than water. Explain why, in terms of the forces holding its particles together.
solution: Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of alternating $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions, each attracted electrostatically to several oppositely charged neighbours.
Melting requires enough energy to overcome these strong electrostatic attractions throughout the whole lattice, not just one bond, which needs a large amount of energy and so a high temperature.
Water's particles are held together by much weaker forces between molecules (covered in an earlier lesson), so far less energy is needed to separate them.
worked_examples.interpretation: The explanation rests on 'many strong attractions across the whole lattice', not on the strength of a single ionic bond in isolation.

worked_examples.statement: **Conduction in three states.** A student tests solid potassium bromide, molten potassium bromide, and a potassium bromide solution with a simple conductivity circuit. Predict and explain the result for each.
solution: Solid: ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move, so the solid does not conduct electricity.
Molten: the lattice has broken down and the $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions are free to move, so the liquid conducts.
Solution: dissolving in water also frees the ions to move throughout the solution, so the solution conducts.
worked_examples.interpretation: All three samples contain exactly the same ions; only ion mobility, which depends on state, changes between them.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying the solid 'has no ions' rather than 'has ions that cannot move'.

worked_examples.statement: **Deducing a formula from charge balance (Supplement).** Calcium forms $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ions and chlorine forms $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions. Deduce the formula of calcium chloride.
solution: One $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ion carries charge $+2$; one $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ion carries charge $-1$.
For overall neutral charge, two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions are needed for every one $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ion: $(+2)+2(-1)=0$.
Formula: $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Charge check: $+2+(-1)+(-1)=0$, confirming the formula is balanced.

guided_exercises.statement: Potassium ($2,8,8,1$) reacts with fluorine ($2,7$). Describe the electron transfer, and state the configuration and charge of each resulting ion.
hints: Identify which atom loses an electron and which gains one, based on how close each is to a full outer shell.
Write the new configuration for each ion after the transfer.
Charge = protons - electrons, remembering the sign convention.
guided_exercises.answer: Potassium's single outer electron transfers to fluorine. Potassium ion: $2,8,8$, charge $+1$. Fluoride ion: $2,8$, charge $-1$.
common_errors: Giving fluoride the configuration $2,7,1$ instead of correctly re-filling its outer shell to $2,8$.

guided_exercises.statement: Magnesium chloride, $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$, does not conduct electricity as a solid at room temperature but does conduct when melted. Explain this difference, and state what you would expect for a solution of magnesium chloride dissolved in water.
hints: Identify what kind of particle has to move for a current to flow in an ionic compound.
Compare whether that particle can move in each physical state.
Dissolving breaks up the lattice in the same general way that melting does.
guided_exercises.answer: In the solid, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move, so no current flows. Melting breaks down the lattice and frees the ions to move, allowing conduction. A solution in water would also conduct for the same reason: dissolving breaks up the lattice and the ions are free to move throughout the solution.
common_errors: Saying the solid 'has no charged particles', when the ions are present but simply immobile.

exercises.statement: Lithium ($2,1$) reacts with chlorine ($2,8,7$) to form lithium chloride. State the configuration and charge of the lithium and chloride ions formed, and write the formula of the compound.
exercises.answer: Lithium ion: $2$, charge $+1$. Chloride ion: $2,8,8$, charge $-1$. Formula: $\mathrm{LiCl}$ (charge check: $+1-1=0$).

exercises.statement: Explain, in terms of ions and electrostatic attraction, why ionic compounds generally have high melting points.
exercises.answer: An ionic compound is a giant lattice in which every ion is strongly attracted, electrostatically, to several oppositely charged neighbours throughout the structure. Melting requires overcoming a very large number of these strong attractions at once, which needs a large amount of energy, and therefore a high temperature.

exercises.statement: Potassium forms $\mathrm{K^+}$ ions and oxygen forms $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ions. Use charge balance to deduce the formula of potassium oxide.
exercises.answer: One $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ needs two $\mathrm{K^+}$ ions to balance its charge: $2(+1)+(-2)=0$. Formula: $\mathrm{K_{2}O}$.

exercises.statement: State three properties that are typical of ionic compounds, and name the two conditions under which an ionic compound conducts electricity.
exercises.answer: Typical properties: high melting and boiling points; poor electrical conductivity when solid but good conductivity when molten or in aqueous solution; generally soluble in water. An ionic compound conducts electricity when it is molten and when it is dissolved in water.

exercises.statement: A city uses rock salt (mostly sodium chloride) on icy roads, partly because dissolving it in the thin layer of water on the road lowers its freezing point. A student claims that salted road water should not conduct electricity, 'because road water is mostly just water, not a solid metal.' Using what you know about ionic compounds, evaluate this claim.
exercises.answer: The claim is incorrect. Dissolving sodium chloride in water releases $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions, which become free to move throughout the water; a metal is not required for conduction, only mobile charged particles. Salted road water would be expected to conduct electricity because of these mobile ions, even though it contains no metal in the electrical sense.

exam_questions.statement: Magnesium reacts with chlorine to form magnesium chloride. (a) State the electron configuration of a magnesium atom and a chlorine atom. (b) Describe the electron transfer that occurs, and give the configuration and charge of each ion formed. (c) Use charge balance to deduce the formula of magnesium chloride.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Magnesium: $2,8,2$. Chlorine: $2,8,7$. (b) Magnesium loses both outer electrons; one electron transfers to each of two separate chlorine atoms. Magnesium ion: $2,8$, charge $+2$. Each chloride ion: $2,8,8$, charge $-1$. (c) One $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ needs two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ for charge balance: $(+2)+2(-1)=0$, giving $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$.
mark_scheme: States Mg configuration 2,8,2.
States Cl configuration 2,8,7.
Describes magnesium losing 2 electrons to two chlorine atoms.
States $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ configuration 2,8 and charge +2.
States $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ configuration 2,8,8 and charge -1 (each).
Deduces formula $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$ from charge balance.

exam_questions.statement: A technician tests solid lead bromide and then molten lead bromide with the same conductivity circuit, getting no reading for the solid and a clear reading for the liquid. Explain this result fully, referring to the particles present and their ability to move in each state.
exam_questions.answer: Lead bromide is an ionic compound made of $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions arranged in a giant lattice. In the solid, these ions are held firmly in fixed positions by strong electrostatic attraction and cannot move to carry charge, so no current is detected. When melted, the lattice structure breaks down and the ions become free to move throughout the liquid; their movement towards the oppositely charged electrodes is what allows a current to be detected.
mark_scheme: Identifies lead bromide as ionic, made of $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions.
States that solid ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move.
States that melting breaks down the lattice.
States that the free-moving ions carry the current in the liquid.
Links the result (no reading vs a reading) explicitly to ion mobility rather than ion presence.

exam_questions.statement: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. (a) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the ions in magnesium oxide. Show only the outer shell of each ion, and include square brackets and charges. (b) State the formula of magnesium oxide.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Magnesium ($2,8,2$) loses both of its outer-shell electrons, so the magnesium ion is drawn as an empty outer shell inside square brackets, with a $2+$ charge outside them. Oxygen ($2,6$) gains those two electrons, so the oxide ion is drawn with eight outer-shell electrons, its own six shown as crosses plus the two from magnesium shown as dots, inside square brackets with a $2-$ charge outside them. (b) $\mathrm{MgO}$, since $(+2)+(-2)=0$.
mark_scheme: Magnesium ion drawn with an empty outer shell (both outer electrons removed).
Oxide ion drawn with eight outer-shell electrons, the two transferred ones shown as dots and the other six as crosses.
Both ions enclosed in square brackets with the charges 2+ and 2- written outside.
States the formula $\mathrm{MgO}$.

challenge_questions.statement: Aluminium forms $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ ions and oxygen forms $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ions. Use charge balance to deduce the formula of aluminium oxide, showing that your answer gives an overall charge of zero.
hints: Find the smallest whole numbers of each ion whose total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
Try small multiples of 3 for aluminium and 2 for oxygen, since the charges are +3 and -2.
challenge_questions.answer: Two $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ ions give $+6$; three $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ions give $-6$; total charge $=+6-6=0$. Formula: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$.
common_errors: Writing $\mathrm{AlO}$ or $\mathrm{Al_{3}O_{2}}$ by matching the numbers 3 and 2 directly to subscripts instead of finding a true common multiple of the charges.

mcq.stem: What happens to the outer electron(s) of a sodium atom when it reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride?

options.text: The electron is shared equally between sodium and chlorine.
options.why_wrong: sharing electrons is covalent bonding; in ionic bonding the electron is transferred, not shared.

options.text: The electron transfers completely from sodium to chlorine.
Sodium gains an electron from chlorine.
options.why_wrong: this reverses the direction; sodium (close to an empty outer shell) loses an electron, it does not gain one.

options.text: No electrons move; only the atoms' positions change.
options.why_wrong: ionic bonding is defined by the formation of ions through electron transfer; without electron movement, no ions would form.

mcq.explanation: Sodium's single outer electron transfers fully to chlorine, forming $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$.

mcq.stem: Which statement best describes solid sodium chloride?

options.text: Individual $\mathrm{NaCl}$ molecules, each a separate pair of ions.
options.why_wrong: there is no individual $\mathrm{NaCl}$ particle; each ion has several neighbours of opposite charge, not just one.

options.text: A giant lattice of neutral $\mathrm{NaCl}$ units joined by weak forces.
options.why_wrong: the lattice is made of charged ions, not neutral units, and the forces between them are strong electrostatic attractions, not weak ones.

options.text: A giant lattice of alternating $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions.
Separate sodium atoms and chlorine molecules mixed together.
options.why_wrong: this describes a mixture of elements, not the ionic compound that actually forms when sodium reacts with chlorine.

mcq.explanation: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice with each ion surrounded by several ions of opposite charge, not isolated pairs.

mcq.stem: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?

options.text: Free electrons released from the ions move through the liquid.
options.why_wrong: ionic compounds have no sea of free electrons; it is the ions themselves that move.

options.text: The liquid contains dissolved metal atoms that conduct like a wire.
options.why_wrong: no metal atoms are present; sodium exists only as $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ions once it has reacted.

options.text: Heat itself carries the current, independent of any charged particle.
options.why_wrong: an electric current always requires the movement of charged particles; heat alone cannot carry charge.

options.text: Mobile $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions carry the charge.

mcq.explanation: Melting frees the $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions to move; their movement towards the electrodes is the electric current.

mcq.stem: Magnesium forms $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ions and fluorine forms $\mathrm{F^-}$ ions. What is the formula of magnesium fluoride?

options.text: $\mathrm{MgF_{2}}$
$\mathrm{MgF}$
options.why_wrong: this would leave a net charge of $+1$, not zero; one $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ needs two $\mathrm{F^-}$ ions to balance.

options.text: $\mathrm{Mg_{2}F}$
options.why_wrong: this gives a net charge of $+3$, since two $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ions would need four $\mathrm{F^-}$ ions, not one, to balance.

options.text: $\mathrm{Mg_{2}F_{2}}$
