options.why_wrong: graphite also conducts as a solid without being a metal, so conduction alone does not prove metallic bonding.

options.text: The solid cannot contain any covalent bonds.
options.why_wrong: graphite conducts and contains covalent bonds within its layers; covalent bonding and conduction are not mutually exclusive.

options.text: The solid has no ions present at all.
options.why_wrong: the observation does not rule out ions being present; it only tells us that some charged particle is mobile, without identifying which.

mcq.explanation: Conduction only proves that some mobile charged particle is present; identifying which one (electron sea, delocalised electron, or, if molten/dissolved, mobile ions) needs further evidence about the structure.

flashcards.front: What is metallic bonding?
flashcards.back: The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions in a giant lattice and a surrounding sea of delocalised electrons.

flashcards.front: Why do metals conduct electricity well?
flashcards.back: Their delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole lattice, carrying charge when a voltage is applied.

flashcards.front: Why are metals malleable (can be bent without shattering)?
flashcards.back: The delocalised electron sea has no fixed direction and redistributes as ion layers slide, so the metallic bond is maintained throughout the deformation.

flashcards.front: Does every solid that conducts electricity have to be a metal?
flashcards.back: No. Graphite (giant covalent) also conducts, using one delocalised electron per carbon atom, without having any metal ions.

flashcards.front: Name the mobile charged particle responsible for conduction in: a metal, graphite, and a molten ionic compound.
flashcards.back: Metal: delocalised electrons (electron sea). Graphite: one delocalised electron per carbon atom. Molten ionic compound: mobile ions.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A metal is a giant structure of neutral metal molecules, similar to a giant covalent structure.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Metals are giant, solid, and extremely strong, which learners associate with the giant covalent structures just studied, overlooking that the particles in a metal are charged ions, not neutral atoms sharing localised bonds.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a metal as made of 'metal molecules' or says the particles in a metal are electrically neutral.
misconceptions.correct_model: A metal is a giant lattice of positively charged metal ions, not neutral atoms or molecules, held together by their electrostatic attraction to a surrounding 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly where each metal atom's outer electron(s) have gone, and establish that they have left the atom (making it a positive ion) to join the shared, moving pool of delocalised electrons.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When a metal is bent or hammered into shape, the positive ions slide past each other without the delocalised electrons being involved at all.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Malleability is pictured as a purely mechanical, 'ions-only' sliding process, since the electrons are imagined as being somewhere else, not actually holding the structure together as the ions move.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes malleability without mentioning the delocalised electrons at all, or implies the metallic bond is temporarily broken while ions slide.
misconceptions.correct_model: The delocalised electrons are not fixed to any one ion, so as layers of positive ions slide into a new arrangement, the electron sea simply flows to surround them in their new positions, and the electrostatic attraction (the metallic bond) is maintained throughout, never fully broken.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast this directly with an ionic lattice: if a layer of ions in an ionic solid is pushed along, ions with the same charge end up next to each other and repel, so the solid shatters. In a metal, the 'glue' (the delocalised electrons) moves along with the rearranged ions, so the attraction is kept and the metal bends instead.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any solid that conducts electricity must have metallic bonding.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Metals are the first and most familiar conductors learners meet, so conduction and 'being a metal' become linked as if one always implies the other.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner classifies graphite as 'a metal' because it conducts electricity, or says molten sodium chloride must be a metal for the same reason.
misconceptions.correct_model: Conduction only requires some mobile charged particle; it can come from delocalised electrons in a metal, delocalised electrons in graphite (a giant covalent structure), or mobile ions in a molten or dissolved ionic compound. Graphite and molten salt both conduct without being metals.
misconceptions.remediation: Build a table of every conductor met in this unit (metal, graphite, molten/aqueous ionic compound) and identify the specific mobile charged particle responsible in each case.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a metal as made of neutral atoms or molecules rather than positive ions.
common_mistakes.why: Metal atoms do not visibly 'look' charged, and the ion-forming step (losing outer electrons) is easy to skip over mentally.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that every metal atom has become a positive ion, and name where its lost electron(s) went (the delocalised sea).

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining malleability without mentioning the delocalised electrons at all.
common_mistakes.why: The ion movement is the visually obvious part of bending a metal; the electrons' role is less obvious.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always state that the electron sea redistributes with the moving ions, keeping the bond intact.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming conduction always means a substance is a metal.
common_mistakes.why: Metals are the first and most familiar conductors learners meet.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name the specific mobile charged particle in each case (delocalised electrons in a metal or in graphite; mobile ions in a molten/dissolved ionic compound) before concluding anything about bonding type.

exam_notes: A metallic bonding description must name both particles (positive ions, delocalised electrons) and the force (electrostatic attraction) between them, not just say 'metallic bonding holds it together'.
A conductivity or malleability explanation should trace the property back to electron or ion mobility specifically, never to bond 'strength' alone.
A comparison question across structure types is best answered with the specific particles and their mobility in each case, not a single memorised rule.

summary.big_idea: A metal is a giant lattice of positive ions held by electrostatic attraction to a mobile sea of delocalised electrons, and this single model explains both metallic conductivity and malleability; across all four bonding models in this unit, every property traces back to specific particles and whether they can move.
key_points: Metallic bonding: electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Metals conduct because the electron sea is free to move through the whole lattice.
Metals are malleable because the electron sea redistributes as ion layers slide, keeping the bond intact.
Conduction always needs some mobile charged particle; it is not always a sign of metallic bonding (graphite is a counterexample).
Every structure-property link in this unit (ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent, metallic) is explained by naming the particles present and their mobility.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Name the mobile charged particle (delocalised electrons or mobile ions) before explaining any conductivity, and remember that not every conductor is a metal.

exit_check.question: A new alloy conducts electricity well and can be rolled into thin sheets without cracking. Explain both properties using the metallic bonding model.
exit_check.answer: Both properties come from the same delocalised electron sea: it provides mobile charge carriers throughout the lattice (good electrical conduction), and because it has no fixed direction, it redistributes as the positive ion layers are rolled into a new, flatter arrangement, keeping the electrostatic attraction intact rather than letting the structure crack (malleability).

epistemic_overrides.note: The "sea of electrons" model is a simplification. Real metallic bonding involves band theory. The model should be marked as MODEL.

summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from atoms elements and bonding accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: Define the following terms using specific examples to help with your explanation: (a) element (b) metal (c) non-metal.
exercises.answer: (a) Element: a substance made up of only one type of atom that cannot be broken down into anything chemically simpler, e.g. aluminium (Al), which consists only of aluminium atoms. (b) Metal: an element that is typically shiny, malleable, ductile, a good conductor of heat and electricity, and generally has a high density, melting point and boiling point, e.g. copper (Cu) or iron (Fe). (c) Non-metal: an element that is typically dull in appearance, brittle if solid, a poor conductor of heat and electricity, and generally has a low density, melting point and boiling point, e.g. sulfur (S) or nitrogen (N).
exercises.full_solution: An element is defined (following Robert Boyle's definition, extended with atomic theory) as a substance that cannot be split into a simpler substance by a chemical reaction, because it contains only one kind of atom; aluminium is a good example since every particle in a sample of aluminium metal is an aluminium atom, and you can only build more complex substances (aluminium oxide, aluminium sulfate) from it, never simplify it further. Elements are then sub-classified as metals or non-metals according to their physical properties (the supplied information/C3.2 in the chapter). A metal such as copper or iron is shiny (has 'metallic lustre'), can be hammered into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile), conducts heat and electricity well, and (with some exceptions, e.g. mercury) tends to have a high density and high melting/boiling point because of strong metallic bonding between its atoms. A non-metal such as sulfur or nitrogen behaves oppositely: solid non-metals are usually dull and brittle rather than malleable, none of them conduct electricity well (graphite is the well-known exception), and as a group they have much lower densities, melting points and boiling points than metals, because the forces holding their particles together (molecular/covalent structures) are generally weaker than metallic bonding.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Which of the substances listed below are: (a) metallic elements (b) non-metallic elements? silicon, chromium, chlorine, iron, copper, sulfur, nitrogen, zinc
exercises.answer: Metallic elements: chromium, iron, copper, zinc. Non-metallic elements: silicon, chlorine, sulfur, nitrogen.
exercises.full_solution: Each substance is a pure element, so it is simply a matter of recalling (or looking up) its position in the Periodic Table. Chromium, iron, copper and zinc are all transition metals: they are shiny, conduct electricity and heat well, and have the characteristic high melting points/densities of metals (consistent with the supplied information, which lists iron and copper this way). Silicon, chlorine, sulfur and nitrogen are all non-metals: chlorine and nitrogen are gases at room temperature with low boiling points, sulfur is a dull brittle yellow solid, and silicon — although it looks shiny and is a semiconductor — is classified as a non-metal in this course (the question itself later describes silicon as 'a Group 4 non-metal element'), because it is brittle rather than malleable and its giant covalent structure behaves chemically like other non-metals rather than like a metal.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Make a list of some other common mixtures, stating what they are mixtures of.
exercises.answer: Example answers: air (a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, argon and water vapour); sea water (water with dissolved salts, mainly sodium chloride); crude oil (a mixture of many different hydrocarbons); brass (an alloy/mixture of copper and zinc); soil (a mixture of sand, clay, decayed organic matter, water and minerals); salad dressing (oil mixed with vinegar/water).
exercises.full_solution: A mixture contains two or more substances that are simply mixed together without reacting chemically, so each listed example must name the separate substances that make it up. Air is a mixture of gaseous elements and compounds (nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, argon, water vapour) that can be separated by fractional distillation of liquid air. Sea water is a mixture of water (a compound) with various dissolved salts, chiefly sodium chloride, separable by evaporation/distillation. Crude oil is a mixture of hundreds of different hydrocarbon compounds, separable by fractional distillation because they have different boiling points. Brass is a mixture (alloy) of the metallic elements copper and zinc, with no fixed ratio, so its composition can vary — exactly the mixture property described in the supplied information. Any similar answer that correctly names the components is acceptable, since this is an open 'give examples' question.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Make a list of some other common compounds, stating the elements they contain and giving the chemical formulae for them.
exercises.answer: Example answers: water, H2O (hydrogen and oxygen); carbon dioxide, CO2 (carbon and oxygen); sodium chloride, NaCl (sodium and chlorine); calcium carbonate, CaCO3 (calcium, carbon and oxygen); ammonia, NH3 (nitrogen and hydrogen); glucose, C6H12O6 (carbon, hydrogen and oxygen).
exercises.full_solution: A compound is a single substance formed when two or more elements chemically combine in a fixed ratio, so each example needs (i) a real compound name/formula and (ii) the elements that have combined inside it, in the correct whole-number ratio shown by the formula's subscripts. Water, H2O, is hydrogen and oxygen combined 2:1; carbon dioxide, CO2, is carbon and oxygen combined 1:2; sodium chloride, NaCl, is sodium and chlorine combined 1:1 (an ionic compound, Na+ and Cl-); calcium carbonate, CaCO3, contains calcium, carbon and oxygen in a fixed 1:1:3 ratio; ammonia, NH3, is nitrogen and hydrogen combined 1:3; glucose, C6H12O6, contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in a 6:12:6 (i.e. 1:2:1) ratio. Unlike the mixtures in Q3, each of these compounds always has exactly this fixed composition and can only be split back into its elements by a chemical reaction, which is the key distinguishing property being tested.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Calculate the number of neutrons in the following atoms: (a) $^{27}_{13}\text{Al}$ (b) $^{31}_{15}\text{P}$ (c) $^{262}_{107}\text{Uus}$ (d) $^{190}_{76}\text{Os}$
exercises.answer: (a) 14 neutrons. (b) 16 neutrons. (c) 155 neutrons. (d) 114 neutrons.
exercises.full_solution: For any atom written as $^{A}_{Z}X$, the mass number A is the total count of protons plus neutrons, and the proton number Z is the number of protons, so the number of neutrons is simply $A - Z$. (a) Aluminium: $27 - 13 = 14$ neutrons. (b) Phosphorus: $31 - 15 = 16$ neutrons. (c) For the nuclide given as $^{262}_{107}\text{Uus}$: $262 - 107 = 155$ neutrons. (Note: the symbol in the question is out of date — element 107 is now called bohrium, Bh; 'Uus' was the temporary name of element 117. The method and the answer, 155, are unaffected.) (d) Osmium: $190 - 76 = 114$ neutrons.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: (a) Define the terms: proton, neutron and electron. (b) An atom X has a proton number of 19 and relative atomic mass of 39. (i) How many electrons, protons and neutrons are there in an atom of X? (ii) How many electrons will there be in the outer energy level (shell) of an atom of X? (iii) What is the electronic configuration of X?
exercises.answer: (a) Proton: a positively charged particle found in the nucleus, with a relative mass of 1. Neutron: an uncharged (neutral) particle found in the nucleus, with a relative mass of 1. Electron: a negatively charged particle, with negligible mass (about 1/1840 of a proton), found moving around the nucleus in energy levels (shells). (b)(i) X is potassium (K): 19 protons, 19 electrons, and 39 - 19 = 20 neutrons. (ii) 1 electron in the outer shell. (iii) Electronic configuration 2,8,8,1.
exercises.full_solution: (a) These are the three sub-atomic particles: the proton (charge +1, relative mass 1) and neutron (charge 0, relative mass 1) sit together in the tiny, dense nucleus, while the much lighter electron (charge -1, negligible mass) occupies the much larger volume of space around the nucleus in defined energy levels. (b) A neutral atom always has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so a proton number of 19 means X has 19 protons and 19 electrons; the relative atomic mass (≈ mass number for a single simple isotope) is protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 39 - 19 = 20 (checked: 39-19=20). Proton number 19 identifies X as potassium. Filling the energy levels 2, then 8, then 8, then whatever remains (following the same pattern as calcium and the other elements in the supplied information) uses up 2+8+8 = 18 electrons, leaving 19-18 = 1 electron for the fourth shell, giving the electronic configuration 2,8,8,1 and therefore 1 electron in the outer (fourth) shell — consistent with potassium being in Group I of the Periodic Table.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: $^{69}_{31}\text{Ga}$ and $^{71}_{31}\text{Ga}$ are isotopes of gallium. With reference to this example, explain what you understand by the term isotope.
exercises.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same proton/atomic number, here 31, so both are gallium and have identical chemical properties) that have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers. $^{60}_{31}$Ga has 60 - 31 = 29 neutrons, while $^{71}_{31}$Ga has 71 - 31 = 40 neutrons; both have 31 protons and 31 electrons.
exercises.full_solution: Isotopes are defined as atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons (and hence the same number of electrons and the same chemical behaviour, since chemistry is governed by the outer-shell electrons) but different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus, which makes their mass numbers different. Applying this to the example: both nuclides have proton number 31, confirming both are gallium atoms with 31 protons and 31 electrons each; the difference lies only in the neutrons, found by mass number minus proton number — $60-31=29$ neutrons for the first, and $71-31=40$ neutrons for the second. The extra neutrons change the mass and mass-dependent properties (such as density) but not the chemical reactivity, because the number of electrons, and particularly the outer-shell electrons, is unchanged. (Note: the common natural isotopes of gallium are gallium-69 and gallium-71; gallium-69 is a naturally occurring stable isotope, but the reasoning is identical.)
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: How many electrons may be accommodated in the first three energy levels?
exercises.answer: First energy level (shell): up to 2 electrons. Second energy level: up to 8 electrons. Third energy level: up to 18 electrons. (For the first 20 elements, which is all this course needs, the third shell holds 8 electrons before the fourth shell starts to fill — e.g. argon 2,8,8 and potassium 2,8,8,1.)
exercises.full_solution: the question states the maximum capacities directly: the first energy level holds up to 2 electrons, the second up to 8, and the third up to 18. You can see the first two in the supplied information: the first shell fills and closes at helium (2), and the second shell fills at neon (2,8). The third shell is different: once it contains 8 electrons (argon, 2,8,8) the atom gains a certain stability, so the next two electrons go into the fourth shell (potassium 2,8,8,1; calcium 2,8,8,2), and only after that do the remaining 10 electrons complete the third shell (in the transition elements). So the answer is 2, 8 and 18 — but for the first 20 elements, which is what IGCSE uses, you write the third shell with a maximum of 8 before starting the fourth.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: What is the same about the electron structures of: (a) lithium, sodium and potassium (b) beryllium, magnesium and calcium?
exercises.answer: (a) Lithium (2,1), sodium (2,8,1) and potassium (2,8,8,1) all have exactly 1 electron in their outer energy level. (b) Beryllium (2,2), magnesium (2,8,2) and calcium (2,8,8,2) all have exactly 2 electrons in their outer energy level.
exercises.full_solution: Using the electron structures in Tables C3.8-C3.10: lithium is 2,1; sodium is 2,8,1; potassium is 2,8,8,1 — in every case the very last number (the outer shell) is 1, so what these three elements have in common is a single outer-shell electron, which is exactly why they are all placed in Group I of the Periodic Table and share similar chemical properties (e.g. all react to form +1 ions). Likewise beryllium is 2,2; magnesium is 2,8,2; calcium is 2,8,8,2 — again the outer shell always holds 2 electrons, placing all three in Group II. This illustrates the general rule given in the chapter: the number of outer-shell electrons matches the Periodic Table group number, and elements in the same group have similar outer-shell electron counts and hence similar chemistry.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Draw diagrams to represent the bonding in each of the following covalent compounds: (a) tetrachloromethane (CCl4) (b) oxygen gas (O2) (c) hydrogen sulfide (H2S) (d) hydrogen chloride (HCl) (e) ethane (C2H6).
exercises.answer: (a) CCl4: one carbon atom (4 outer electrons) in the centre, joined to four separate chlorine atoms (7 outer electrons each) by four single covalent bonds (one shared electron pair each); carbon ends up with a share of 8 electrons and each chlorine ends up with a share of 8. (b) O2: the two oxygen atoms (6 outer electrons each) share two pairs of electrons between them, forming one double covalent bond (O=O), so each oxygen atom has a share of 8 electrons. (c) H2S: a central sulfur atom (6 outer electrons) forms two single covalent bonds, one to each of two hydrogen atoms; sulfur ends with a share of 8 electrons, each hydrogen with a share of 2. (d) HCl: one single covalent bond between H (1 outer electron) and Cl (7 outer electrons), giving H a share of 2 electrons and Cl a share of 8. (e) C2H6: the two carbon atoms are joined to each other by one single covalent C-C bond, and each carbon also forms three single covalent C-H bonds to its own hydrogen atoms; each carbon therefore has a share of 8 electrons (4 bonds), and each hydrogen has a share of 2.
exercises.full_solution: In each case the diagram is a 'dot-and-cross' picture showing only the outer-shell electrons, with the electrons from one atom drawn as dots and from the other as crosses, and a shared pair (one dot + one cross, overlapping between the two atoms' circles) representing one single covalent bond. The rule used throughout is that each atom shares enough electron pairs to end up with a stable, full outer shell (8 electrons — an octet — for all these atoms except hydrogen, which only needs 2, a duplet, to match helium). (a) Carbon has 4 outer electrons and needs 4 more, so it forms 4 single bonds, one to each of 4 chlorine atoms, each of which has 7 outer electrons and needs only 1 more, giving the familiar tetrahedral CCl4 molecule. (b) Each oxygen atom has 6 outer electrons and needs 2 more; sharing just one pair would only bring each atom to 7, so the two oxygens must share two pairs (4 electrons total, 2 from each atom) — a double bond — which brings each one up to 8. (c) Sulfur, like oxygen, has 6 outer electrons and needs 2 more, but here it gets these from two separate hydrogen atoms (1 electron each) rather than from one double bond, giving two single S-H bonds. (d) Hydrogen (1 electron) and chlorine (7 electrons) simply share one pair, satisfying both (H reaches 2, Cl reaches 8). (e) In ethane each carbon has 4 outer electrons; one of its four bonds goes to the other carbon atom (a C-C single bond) and the remaining three bonds go to three separate hydrogen atoms (three C-H single bonds), so every carbon atom ends up participating in 4 shared pairs (octet) and every hydrogen atom in 1 shared pair (duplet).
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: The diagram (Figure, dot-and-cross structure) shows the arrangement of the outer electrons only in a molecule of ethanoic acid (CH3COOH): a left-hand carbon atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms and to a second (right-hand) carbon atom, which is in turn double-bonded to one oxygen atom and singly bonded to a second oxygen atom that is bonded to a hydrogen atom. (a) Name the different elements found in this compound. (b) What is the total number of atoms present in this molecule? (c) Between which two atoms is there a double covalent bond? (d) How many single covalent bonds does each carbon atom have? (e) Write a paragraph explaining the sorts of properties you would expect this substance to have.
exercises.answer: (a) Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. (b) 8 atoms in total (2 C + 4 H + 2 O). (c) Between the right-hand (carboxyl) carbon atom and the oxygen atom drawn above it (a C=O double bond). (d) The left-hand (methyl) carbon has 4 single covalent bonds (3 C-H bonds plus the C-C bond); the right-hand (carboxyl) carbon has 2 single covalent bonds (the C-C bond and a C-O bond to the -OH oxygen) in addition to its C=O double bond. (e) As a simple molecular (covalent) substance it should have a relatively low melting/boiling point compared with an ionic compound, should not conduct electricity as a pure liquid, and should dissolve well in water (because of its polar -OH and C=O groups, which allow hydrogen bonding with water and some ionisation to release H+ ions, since ethanoic acid is a weak acid).
exercises.full_solution: Reading the molecule's formula directly from the diagram, CH3COOH (= C2H4O2), gives (a) three elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. (b) Counting every circle in the diagram: 2 carbon atoms + 4 hydrogen atoms (3 on the left-hand carbon, 1 on the right-hand oxygen) + 2 oxygen atoms = 8 atoms altogether. (c) A double covalent bond is drawn wherever two pairs of electrons (four dots/crosses) are shared between the same two atoms; in this structure that only happens between the right-hand carbon and the oxygen drawn directly above it, i.e. the C=O of the carboxyl group. (d) Counting bonds atom by atom: the left-hand carbon forms 4 separate single bonds — three to its three hydrogen atoms and one to the other carbon atom; the right-hand carbon forms the C=O double bond already identified in (c), plus 2 single bonds — one back to the left-hand carbon and one to the -OH oxygen. (e) Because every bond inside the molecule is a strong covalent bond but the molecules themselves are only held to each other by comparatively weak intermolecular forces, ethanoic acid is expected to behave like other small covalent molecules: a low-ish melting point and boiling point (real ethanoic acid melts at about 17°C and boils at about 118°C, both far below those of an ionic solid), no electrical conductivity in its pure molecular form (there are no free ions or delocalised electrons), but good solubility in water, since the polar O-H and C=O bonds let it hydrogen-bond with water molecules and let a small fraction of molecules ionise to release H+(aq) ions — which is exactly why ethanoic acid behaves as a (weak) acid in solution.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Explain why graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not.
exercises.answer: In graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to only 3 neighbouring carbon atoms (not 4), so one outer-shell electron per atom is left over; these spare electrons become delocalised and are free to move along the layers of carbon atoms, carrying electric current. In diamond, every carbon atom is covalently bonded to 4 other carbon atoms, using up all 4 of its outer electrons in fixed, localised bonds, so there are no free/delocalised electrons available to carry a current and diamond does not conduct electricity.
exercises.full_solution: Electrical conduction in a solid requires charge carriers (such as free electrons or mobile ions) that can move through the structure. Diamond has a rigid, three-dimensional giant covalent structure in which every carbon atom uses all 4 of its outer-shell electrons to form 4 strong, localised single covalent bonds to 4 neighbouring carbon atoms; because every electron is tied up in a fixed bond between two specific atoms, none are free to move, so diamond cannot conduct electricity (it behaves as an electrical insulator). Graphite, by contrast, has a layered structure in which each carbon atom only forms 3 covalent bonds (to 3 neighbours within the same flat layer); this uses only 3 of its 4 outer electrons, leaving the fourth electron from each atom delocalised across the layer, free to move along the layers of atoms when a voltage is applied. It is this 'sea' of mobile, delocalised electrons — similar in effect to the free electrons in a metal — that lets graphite conduct electricity along its layers, even though both substances are made of exactly the same element, carbon.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: From your knowledge of the structure of silicon dioxide and diamond predict the following properties of silicon dioxide: hardness, melting and boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility.
exercises.answer: Silicon dioxide should be: very hard (though less hard than diamond); have a very high melting point and boiling point (quartz actually melts at about 1610°C and boils at about 2230°C); not conduct electricity (in any state); and be insoluble in both water and organic solvents.
exercises.full_solution: Silicon dioxide (silica/quartz) has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure built from a tetrahedral network of Si and O atoms, directly analogous to the tetrahedral all-carbon network in diamond, so its physical properties can be predicted by the same reasoning used for diamond. Hardness and melting/boiling point: because every atom is locked into the 3-D network by strong covalent Si-O bonds that extend throughout the whole crystal, an enormous number of strong bonds must be broken to melt or shatter the solid, so — just like diamond — silicon dioxide is predicted to be very hard with a very high melting point and boiling point; this matches the real data given for quartz (melting point 1610°C, boiling point 2230°C), though it is somewhat less hard than diamond (its network of Si-O-Si links is less compact and rigid than diamond's network of C-C bonds). Electrical conductivity: as in diamond, all of the outer-shell electrons of the silicon and oxygen atoms are used up forming the covalent bonds of the network, leaving no free or delocalised electrons (and no ions) to carry a current, so silicon dioxide is predicted to be a non-conductor of electricity, which is indeed the case. Solubility: because the atoms are held by strong covalent bonds throughout a giant 3-D lattice rather than existing as separate small molecules, there is no way for solvent molecules (polar water or non-polar organic solvents) to separate out individual 'molecules' of silicon dioxide, so — again like diamond — it is predicted to be insoluble in both water and organic solvents.
